15071:
El is simply the old West Semitic word for 'god', and also the name of the high god who ruled over all the other gods in Canaanite religion. At Ugarit he is a wise, grey-bearded father figure who sits enthroned and hands down decisions to a council of younger gods.

The Bible uses the same word constantly for Israel's God (El Shaddai, El Elyon, Bethel = 'house of El', Israel = perhaps 'El strives'). Unlike Baal, El is almost never attacked in the Bible. That is because Israel's writers treated El either as an ordinary word for God or as another name of the one God they worshipped. How much of Canaanite El was absorbed into Israel's picture of Yahweh is a real and open question among scholars.
15072:
In the clay tablets from Ugarit (14th to 13th century BC), El is 'Father of Years', 'Bull El', 'Creator of Creatures' and 'Kind El, the Compassionate'. He lives in a tent-shrine on a mountain at the springs of the two rivers and the two deeps. The gods are his children and meet in 'the assembly of El'.

El does not fight. He decides. When Yam (Sea) wants supremacy, El grants it; when Baal needs a palace, Baal and Anat must win El's permission, usually by going through his wife Athirat. Anat even threatens the old god to get her way. When Baal dies, El comes down from his throne, sits in the dust, gashes his skin and mourns. Then he dreams that the heavens rain oil and the wadis run with honey, and knows that Baal lives again. One text (the 'Birth of the Gracious Gods') describes El fathering gods in a frank, earthy scene by the sea.
15073:
El is the one Canaanite god the Bible does not fight. The patriarchs meet God under El names: El Elyon ('God Most High', Gen 14:18-22), El Roi (Gen 16:13), El Shaddai (Gen 17:1), El Olam (Gen 21:33), El-Elohe-Israel (Gen 33:20). Exod 6:3 says God appeared to the patriarchs as El Shaddai but was not known to them by the name Yahweh.

Some biblical poetry describes God with language that matches El at Ugarit: an aged figure on a throne with white hair (Dan 7:9), the 'divine assembly' (Ps 82:1, adat-el), and the Most High dividing the nations (Deut 32:8). Melchizedek's title for God, 'Most High, creator (or possessor) of heaven and earth' (Gen 14:19), matches a Phoenician title of El found at Karatepe.

How to read this is debated. (1) Many critical scholars (Frank Moore Cross, Mark S. Smith) argue that Yahweh and El were originally separate gods and that Israel merged them, so that Yahweh took over El's role as head of the council. (2) Others argue Israel always used 'El' as a generic word and title for its own God, so the overlap is about shared language, not borrowed gods. (3) Traditional Jewish and Christian readers see the patriarchs worshipping the one true God under the common word for God, with the name Yahweh revealed more fully at the exodus.

15075: The priest-king of Salem blesses Abram by 'God Most High, creator of heaven and earth', and Abram identifies this God with Yahweh in his oath.

15077: Jacob names places after El: Bethel ('house of El') and El-Elohe-Israel ('El, the God of Israel').
15079: God tells Moses that he appeared to the patriarchs as El Shaddai, but by the name Yahweh he did not make himself known to them.
15080: The Most High divides the nations
15081: Elyon apportions the nations, and Yahweh's portion is Jacob. Whether Elyon and Yahweh are the same figure here is debated; most traditional readers say yes.

15083: God takes his stand in the 'assembly of El' and judges the gods. The phrase matches Ugaritic language for El's council.
15084: Daniel sees an aged figure with white hair enthroned among a court, a picture many scholars compare to El, the Father of Years.

15099: El never became a demon. The word simply lived on: in Hebrew as a term for God, in names like Israel, Samuel, Michael, Gabriel and Immanuel, and in the related Aramaic elah and Arabic ilah (from which Allah derives). In Phoenician religion of the first millennium El faded behind city gods like Melqart and Baal Shamem; Philo of Byblos (via Eusebius) equated him with the Greek Kronos.

15120:
Asherah was the great mother-goddess of Canaan, wife of the high god El. In the Bible the word 'asherah' means two connected things: the goddess herself, and a wooden pole or stylised tree set up beside altars to stand for her. That is why the Bible talks about asherahs being 'made', 'planted', 'cut down' and 'burned'.

What makes Asherah famous today is a set of Hebrew inscriptions from about 800-700 BC that bless people 'by Yahweh and his asherah'. They show that at least some Israelites put Asherah, or her symbol, right next to Israel's God. The prophets and the reforming kings fought this for centuries.
15121: At Ugarit she is Athirat, 'Lady Athirat of the Sea' (the exact meaning of the title is debated, perhaps 'she who treads on the sea'), wife of El and 'creatress of the gods', mother of seventy divine sons. She nurses royal heirs in the Kirta epic. In the Baal Cycle she first sides with Yam against Baal, but when Baal and Anat bring her gifts she rides on a donkey to El's tent and persuades him to let Baal build his palace. After Baal dies, she proposes one of her sons, Athtar, as replacement king; he is too small to fill Baal's throne. So she is the queen mother of heaven: the one who has El's ear.
15122:
Asherah appears about 40 times in the Bible. Most uses are the wooden cult object: Israel is told not to plant any tree as an asherah beside Yahweh's altar (Deut 16:21) and to cut down the Canaanites' asherim (Exod 34:13; Deut 7:5). Gideon cuts down his father's asherah beside the altar of Baal (Judg 6:25-28).

Some passages clearly mean the goddess: 400 'prophets of Asherah' eat at Jezebel's table (1 Kgs 18:19); Josiah removes vessels made 'for Baal and for Asherah' (2 Kgs 23:4). Queen mother Maacah made an 'abominable image for Asherah' and was deposed for it (1 Kgs 15:13). Manasseh put a carved image of Asherah inside Yahweh's temple (2 Kgs 21:7). Josiah took it out, burned it at the Kidron, ground it to dust and threw the dust on the common graves; he also tore down the rooms in the temple where women wove hangings for Asherah (2 Kgs 23:6-7).

The repeated fight suggests Asherah worship was not a foreign import but a deep-rooted part of popular religion in both Israel and Judah. The biblical writers present it as apostasy; many historians see it as the older popular religion that the prophets and reforming kings set out to remove. Both statements can be true at once.
15123: Do not plant an asherah beside Yahweh's altar
15124: The law forbids setting up an asherah or standing stone next to Yahweh's altar, which implies people were doing exactly that.
15125: Gideon cuts down his father's asherah
15126: Gideon tears down his father's Baal altar and the asherah beside it, then uses its wood to burn a sacrifice to Yahweh.
15128: King Asa removes his grandmother from her position because she made an image for Asherah, and burns it at the Kidron.
15130: Ahab makes an asherah in Samaria; Jezebel feeds 450 prophets of Baal and 400 of Asherah. Only Baal's prophets appear at the Carmel contest itself.
15131: Manasseh puts Asherah in the temple
15132: Manasseh sets up a carved image of Asherah in the house where Yahweh had said he would put his name.
15134: Josiah removes the Asherah from the temple, burns and grinds it, scatters its dust on graves, and pulls down the women's weaving rooms. He also cuts down asherim at Bethel and elsewhere.
15136: Prophets list the asherim beside altars on hills and under green trees as part of what brought judgement.
15140: Storage jars at a c. 800 BC caravan way-station carry blessings 'by Yahweh of Samaria and his asherah' and 'by Yahweh of Teman and his asherah'. Drawings on the same jar show two Bes-like figures and a seated lyre player; whether any of them depict Yahweh and Asherah is disputed, and most specialists think the standing pair are Bes figures.
15144: A late 8th-century BC tomb inscription for one Uriyahu says he is blessed by Yahweh and that 'by his asherah' Yahweh saved him from his enemies. The text is damaged and its reading is partly uncertain.
15148: Biblical Hebrew normally does not put a possessive ending ('his') on a personal name, so many read 'his asherah' as Yahweh's cult object, the pole or tree. Others argue the object and the goddess were never really separable, or that the grammar rule has exceptions, so the texts show a belief that Yahweh had a consort. A third view reads it as a place or shrine. The question is unresolved.
15149: Tel Arad shrine and its two altars (residue study 2020)
15152: A small shrine inside a Judahite royal fortress had standing stones and two limestone incense altars at the entrance to its niche. A 2020 study (Arie, Rosen and Namdar, *Tel Aviv*) found frankincense mixed with animal fat on one altar and cannabis mixed with animal dung on the other: the earliest known evidence of a mind-altering substance in Judah's worship. The shrine, dated to the 8th century BC, was deliberately buried; the excavators tied this to Hezekiah's reform, others to Josiah or to other causes. Whether the two stones or altars stood for Yahweh and a consort such as Asherah is an attractive guess, not a finding.
15156: A 10th-century BC clay stand has four tiers: one shows a nude female between two lions, another a sacred tree flanked by ibexes and lions. Many read these as Asherah and her tree symbol (Ruth Hestrin's interpretation); the top tier shows an animal under a winged sun.
15159: Jerusalem, Lachish and many Judahite sites
15160: Hundreds of small clay women holding their breasts, common c. 750-586 BC in Judean homes. Many scholars (e.g. William Dever) link them to Asherah; others see them as generic fertility charms or images of worshippers.
15161: Asherah disappeared from Jewish worship after the exile, but the word survived in strange ways. The Greek Septuagint and Latin Vulgate often translated asherah as 'grove' (alsos, lucus), so the King James Version speaks of 'groves', and generations of readers did not know a goddess lay behind the word. The Mishnah (tractate Avodah Zarah) still discusses what makes a tree an asherah. Asherah has no prominent place in Milton's catalogue or in medieval demon lists. Since the Kuntillet Ajrud discoveries she has become a popular subject in books and documentaries about 'God's wife', a framing that the evidence supports only in part.
15175: Baal Shamem ('lord of heaven', later Phoenician)
15176: Melqart (Baal of Tyre, a related city god)
15182: bull; warrior with raised club and a spear sprouting into lightning
15183: Mount Zaphon (Jebel Aqra), 1,717 m, on the Syrian-Turkish border; temple of Baal on the acropolis of Ugarit
15186: head of the household he belongs to
15194:
'Baal' is not really a name. It is a title meaning 'lord', 'owner' or 'husband'. The god most often meant by it is Hadad, the storm god who brings thunder and, above all, rain.

That matters because of geography. Egypt was watered by the Nile and Mesopotamia by the Tigris and Euphrates. Canaan lived or died by rainfall, as Deuteronomy itself points out (Deut 11:10-11). A god who controlled the rain controlled the harvest, so for farmers Baal was the obvious god to keep happy. The Bible's long struggle against Baal, from Judges to Jeremiah, is a struggle over who really sends the rain.
15195:
The Baal Cycle, six tablets from Ugarit written down by the scribe Ilimilku around the 14th or 13th century BC, tells Baal's story in three episodes.

1. Baal and Yam. Yam (Sea) is made king by El and demands that Baal be handed over. The craftsman god Kothar-wa-Khasis makes Baal two magic clubs, 'Driver' and 'Chaser'. The second strikes Yam down. Baal is acclaimed king.

2. Baal's palace. A king needs a house. With Anat's help and Athirat's persuasion, El allows it, and Kothar builds a palace of gold, silver and lapis on Mount Zaphon. Kothar proposes a window; Baal at first refuses, then agrees, and through it he thunders his voice across the earth. (Why he hesitated is debated; one guess links it to the line 'death has come up into our windows', Jer 9:21.)

3. Baal and Mot. Mot (Death) invites Baal to his realm. Baal goes down into Death's throat and dies; the land dries out. El and Anat mourn; Anat buries him on Zaphon. Anat then seizes Mot, splits him with a blade, winnows, burns, grinds and sows him like grain. El dreams of heavens raining oil, and Baal returns. Seven years later Baal and Mot fight again until the sun goddess Shapash separates them.

Many scholars read this as a seasonal myth of the dry summer and the return of the autumn rains. Others (e.g. Mark S. Smith) caution that it is mainly about kingship and the fragile order of the world, not a neat annual calendar.
15196:
Baal is Yahweh's chief rival in the historical books. Israel 'yoked itself' to Baal-peor in the wilderness (Num 25:3). In Judges, each slide into apostasy is described as serving 'the Baals' (Judg 2:11-13). Gideon tears down his father's Baal altar and is nicknamed Jerubbaal, 'let Baal contend' (Judg 6:25-32).

The big confrontation comes under Ahab, who married Jezebel, daughter of Ethbaal king of the Sidonians, and built a Baal temple in Samaria (1 Kgs 16:31-32). Which Baal Jezebel promoted is debated: Melqart of Tyre, Baal Shamem, or Hadad. Elijah announces a drought: no dew or rain except at his word (1 Kgs 17:1), a direct challenge to the rain god. On Mount Carmel the contest is fought on Baal's home ground: fire from the sky, then rain (1 Kgs 18). Jehu later massacres Baal's worshippers and turns his Samaria temple into a latrine (2 Kgs 10:18-28); in Judah Athaliah's Baal temple falls with her (2 Kgs 11:18).

The prophets keep fighting. Hosea says Israel did not know it was Yahweh who gave the grain, wine and oil she credited to Baal, and that one day she will no longer call God 'my Baal' (Hos 2:8; Hos 2:16-17). Jeremiah, some three centuries after Elijah, still condemns Baal altars and child burning 'to Baal' (Jer 2:23; Jer 19:5).

The Bible also borrows Baal's imagery for Yahweh: the one who 'rides on the clouds' (Ps 68:4; Ps 104:3; Isa 19:1), whose thunderous voice shakes the cedars (Ps 29), and who crushes the sea monster. Many scholars think Ps 29 adapts a Canaanite storm hymn; others see shared regional poetry rather than borrowing. The point in either case is polemical: the titles Baal claimed belong to Yahweh.
15197: The cycle of Judges: 'they served the Baals'
15198: Each generation abandons Yahweh for the Baals and Ashtaroth and falls to its enemies.

15202: Ahab marries the Sidonian princess Jezebel, builds a house of Baal in Samaria and makes an asherah.
15204: Elijah declares no dew or rain except at his word, striking at the storm god's own domain.

Elijah mocks: perhaps he is musing, or has 'turned aside' (possibly a euphemism for relieving himself; debated), or is travelling, or asleep. They gash themselves, a mourning rite; El himself gashes his skin over the dead Baal at Ugarit. Elijah soaks his altar with twelve jars of water; fire falls and consumes it. The people cry, 'Yahweh, he is God.'

15210: Jehu gathers Baal's worshippers into his temple in Samaria, kills them, breaks the pillar and makes the building a latrine.

15214: Israel credited Baal with the grain, wine and oil that Yahweh gave. Hosea plays on ba'al as 'husband': Israel will call God 'my husband' (ishi) instead.
15216: Jeremiah condemns altars to 'the shameful thing' (bosheth), to Baal, and the burning of children 'to Baal' in the Hinnom valley.

15220: A farmer's plough opened a tomb at Minet el-Beida in 1928; digs at Ras Shamra began in 1929 and the first tablets appeared that May. The new alphabetic cuneiform was deciphered in 1930 by Hans Bauer, Edouard Dhorme and Charles Virolleaud. The Baal Cycle (KTU 1.1-1.6) is the fullest account of Baal's myths.

15231: Chronicles keeps the original names of Saul's son and grandson, Eshbaal and Merib-baal (1 Chr 8:33-34). Samuel calls them Ish-bosheth and Mephibosheth (2 Sam 2:8; 2 Sam 4:4), and calls Gideon Jerubbesheth (2 Sam 11:21). Bosheth means 'shame'. The standard explanation is that scribes replaced 'Baal' with 'shame' to avoid saying the god's name; Jeremiah and Hosea themselves call Baal 'the shame' (Jer 11:13; Hos 9:10). In Saul's time 'baal' could still be used innocently of Yahweh as 'lord'. A minority view argues that bosheth was once an honourable divine epithet (compare Akkadian bashtu, 'dignity'), so not every change is an insult.
15232: Hadad survived for centuries in Syria: as Hadad of Damascus (Rimmon), as Zeus Kasios on his old mountain Zaphon (where the Roman emperors Hadrian and Julian are reported to have climbed to sacrifice), and as Jupiter Heliopolitanus at Baalbek in Lebanon, whose name preserves 'Baal'. In Christian thought the Baals became demons. Milton's *Paradise Lost* (Book 1) lists 'Baalim and Ashtaroth' together among the fallen angels, and early modern demon lists include a 'Bael' or 'Baal' as a king of hell. 'Baal' is still used in English as a byword for a false god.

15255:
Anat was Canaan's fiercest goddess: a young warrior who fights for her brother Baal. In one famous scene she slaughters an army and wades knee-deep, then neck-deep, in blood, with severed heads hung at her waist. When Baal dies she hunts down Death himself and destroys him.

The Bible never names her as a goddess, but her name survives in place names and personal names (Anathoth, Jeremiah's home town; Shamgar 'son of Anath'), which shows she was once known in the land.
15256:
In the Baal Cycle Anat battles armies 'from the seashore to the sunrise', wading through blood, then hosts a feast. She threatens El with violence to get Baal his palace. When Baal dies she searches the earth for him, weeps until she is full of tears, carries his body to Zaphon and buries him. Then she seizes Mot and destroys him as a farmer treats grain: she splits him with a blade, winnows him, burns him, grinds him and sows him in the field, and the birds eat his flesh. In the Aqhat epic she covets a magic bow belonging to the young hero Aqhat, offers him immortality for it, is rebuffed, and has him killed, after which the land suffers drought.

She is called 'virgin' or 'maiden', yet some texts seem to describe a sexual union with Baal; whether these are about Anat and what 'virgin' means here are debated.
15257: Anat is not named as a deity in the Hebrew Bible. Her name survives in: Anathoth, a Levitical town and Jeremiah's birthplace (Josh 21:18; Jer 1:1); Beth-anath ('house of Anat') in Naphtali, which the Israelites did not conquer (Josh 19:38; Judg 1:33); and the judge Shamgar 'son of Anath' (Judg 3:31; Judg 5:6), possibly a warrior title ('son of Anat' = a soldier under her protection) rather than his parent's name. Some scholars suggest she is among the candidates for the 'Queen of Heaven' of Jeremiah, since Egyptian texts call her 'lady of heaven'; this is one option among several.
15259: A judge who killed 600 Philistines with an ox-goad bears Anat's name, perhaps as a family name or a warrior title.
15261: A town named 'house of Anat' stood in Naphtali's territory; its Canaanite inhabitants remained.
